title: Max Points on a Line
directAnswer: Find the most points lying on a single straight line. The brute-force triple check is O(n³). The interview answer is O(n²): fix each point as an anchor, then group every other point by the *slope* of the line through it and the anchor using a hash map. Points sharing a slope through the same anchor are collinear. The crux is representing slope **exactly** — store the reduced (dy, dx) vector (divide by gcd, normalize the sign) as the key, never a floating-point division, to dodge precision bugs and vertical-line divide-by-zero.

remember.pattern: Anchor + hash slopes (reduced gcd vector) → most collinear points
remember.formula:
best = 0
for i in range(n):                      # anchor
    slopes = {}
    for j in range(i+1, n):
        dx, dy = x[j]-x[i], y[j]-y[i]
        g = gcd(dx, dy)                 # non-negative
        dx, dy = dx//g, dy//g
        if dx < 0 or (dx == 0 and dy < 0):  # canonical sign
            dx, dy = -dx, -dy
        slopes[(dx, dy)] += 1
        best = max(best, slopes[(dx, dy)] + 1)
return best  (or n if n <= 2)
rules: Represent slope as the **reduced integer vector `(dx/g, dy/g)`**, never `dy/dx` as a float — floating point misjudges near-parallel lines.
Divide `dx` and `dy` by their **gcd** so all points on one line collapse to the *same* key regardless of distance from the anchor.
**Normalize the sign** so `(2,1)` and `(-2,-1)` map to one key — pick `dx > 0`, and for vertical lines (`dx == 0`) force `dy > 0`.
Add **+1** to the bucket count: the bucket counts the *other* points, the anchor itself completes the line.
Handle `n <= 2` up front — any one or two points are trivially collinear; return `n`.
whenToUse: 'Most collinear points' / 'points on the same line' over a set of coordinates
You need an exact geometric relationship (collinearity, same direction) without float error
Grouping by a normalized direction/ratio where a hash map collapses equivalents
n is small-to-moderate so an O(n²) anchor sweep is acceptable
antiSignals: Points are already sorted along a known axis with a special structure → a tailored scan may beat O(n²)
You need lines defined by a fixed direction only → simpler grouping, no per-anchor sweep
Floating-point slope is 'good enough' → it isn't here; collinearity demands exact arithmetic
remember.takeaway: Max Points on a Line is the canonical 'hash an exact ratio' problem. The lesson that transfers: when grouping by a slope, fraction, or direction, never trust floats — reduce to a coprime integer pair with gcd and normalize the sign so equivalent ratios hash together. That exact-ratio trick reappears in Line Reflection, counting parallel segments, and any 'same direction' grouping.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid the O(n³) triple loop by anchoring and hashing slopes, AND whether you represent slope without floating-point error — the gcd-reduced, sign-normalized vector is the real test. Vertical lines and the float-precision trap are the discriminators.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using `(double) dy / dx` as the slope key (precision errors merge distinct lines and crash on vertical dx = 0), or forgetting to normalize the sign so `(1,2)` and `(-1,-2)` split a single line into two buckets.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with 'fix an anchor, hash exact slopes', then immediately raise the precision issue and explain the gcd-reduce-plus-sign-normalize key. Mention vertical and horizontal lines fall out naturally, and that uniqueness lets you skip duplicate handling.

problemStatement: Given an array of `points` where `points[i] = [xi, yi]` represents a point on the X-Y plane, return *the maximum number of points that lie on the same straight line*.
understanding: We want the largest subset of points that are collinear. Two points always define a line, so the answer is at least min(n, 2). The challenge is checking collinearity efficiently and exactly: three points are collinear iff the line through the first two has the same slope as the line through the first and third. Anchoring on one point and bucketing the rest by slope lets us count, for each anchor, the biggest collinear group passing through it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be duplicate points?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the constraints guarantee all points are unique. That simplifies the slope hashing: I never have to add a separate 'same coordinate' count to every line, which older versions of this problem required.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the answer for 0, 1, or 2 points?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: For n ≤ 2 every point trivially lies on one line, so return n. I special-case that before the main loop.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use floating-point slope (dy / dx)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'd avoid it. Floats can't represent most ratios exactly, so near-parallel lines may collide or split, and vertical lines divide by zero. I'll key on the reduced integer vector instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can the coordinates get — do I need to worry about overflow?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Coordinates are within ±10⁴, so differences fit in 32-bit ints and gcd reduction is safe. If I used the cross-product check I'd cast to long to be safe, but the products here stay within int range anyway.

examples.explanation: All three points lie on the line y = x.
The points (1,1), (3,2), (5,3) plus (4,1)… actually the maximal line here passes through 4 of the points; any line can hold at most 4.
(0,0), (1,1), (2,2) are collinear on y = x. (3,1) is off that line, so the max is 3.
A single point is trivially on a line by itself.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Anchoring and hashing exact slopes turns the O(n³) triple check into O(n²) — the float-free slope key is the crux.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Triple (Cross Product)
approaches.whenToMention: State it to anchor the complexity and to introduce the exact (integer) collinearity test, then improve to the O(n²) anchor-hash solution.
hints: Collinearity is a property of three points. What's the most direct way to test whether a third point lies on the line through two others?
For each pair (i, j), count how many other points k are collinear with them. Three points are collinear when the cross product of (j − i) and (k − i) is zero.
Track the maximum count over all pairs. Use the integer cross product `(jx−ix)(ky−iy) − (jy−iy)(kx−ix) == 0` to stay exact and avoid division.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Three nested loops over pairs and a third point give n·n·n = O(n³). Only counters are stored → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
For every pair of points `(i, j)`, walk every remaining point `k` and test whether `i`, `j`, `k` are collinear; count how many lie on that line and track the global maximum.

**The exact collinearity test.** Three points `A`, `B`, `C` are collinear exactly when the vectors `B − A` and `C − A` are parallel, i.e. their 2D cross product is zero: `(Bx − Ax)(Cy − Ay) − (By − Ay)(Cx − Ax) == 0`. This is pure integer arithmetic — **no division, no floats, no divide-by-zero** for vertical lines. That property is the reason to introduce the cross product early; the optimal approach will reuse the same 'compare directions exactly' idea, just bucketed.

**Why it's correct but slow.** Fixing a pair and scanning the rest reliably finds the line through that pair and counts its members. Doing it for *all* pairs guarantees we examine every possible line. But there are `O(n²)` pairs and each scan is `O(n)`, so the total is `O(n³)`. For `n = 300` that's `2.7 × 10⁷` triples — it actually passes here, but it signals you missed the linear-per-anchor grouping.

**The wasted work that motivates the upgrade.** The triple loop recomputes the same line many times: the line through three collinear points is rediscovered from pair `(A,B)`, pair `(A,C)`, and pair `(B,C)` separately. If instead we *group* points by slope around a single anchor, every point on a line is counted once per anchor — collapsing the inner pair-scan into a single hashed pass and dropping a whole factor of `n`.
approaches.insight: The cross product is the float-free heart of all collinearity work: parallel direction vectors ⇔ zero cross product. Keep it in your back pocket — even the optimal hashed solution is just 'group points whose direction vector from the anchor is identical', which is the same parallelism test expressed as a hash key instead of a per-triple computation.

pitfalls: Using a slope ratio with division here instead of the cross product — reintroduces float error and vertical-line divide-by-zero.
Starting `count` at 0 or 1 instead of 2 — the anchor pair is two points.
Forgetting the `n <= 2` guard — the loops never run and you'd return 0.

approaches.name: Anchor + Hash Exact Slopes (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Say 'fix each point as an anchor and bucket the others by an exact slope key', then defend the gcd-reduced, sign-normalized vector against floating point.
hints: Any line that holds many points passes through at least one of them. So fix one point as an anchor — how do you count, in one pass, how many others share a line through it?

Two other points are on the same line through the anchor exactly when they have the same slope relative to the anchor. Bucket points by slope in a hash map; the biggest bucket + 1 (the anchor) is the best line through this anchor.

Represent slope exactly: dx = xj − xi, dy = yj − yi, divide both by gcd(dx, dy), then normalize the sign (make dx > 0; for vertical lines make dy > 0). Use that integer pair as the key — never a float.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer loop fixes each of n anchors; the inner loop hashes the other ≤ n−1 points in O(1) average each → O(n²) time. Each anchor uses a fresh map of up to n−1 slope buckets → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Fix each point `i` as an **anchor**. For every other point `j`, compute the direction vector `(dx, dy) = (xj − xi, yj − yi)` and reduce it to a canonical form that is identical for all points lying on the same line through the anchor. Tally these canonical slopes in a hash map; the largest bucket counts the other points on the best line through `i`, so that line holds `bucket + 1` points (adding the anchor). The global maximum over all anchors is the answer.

**Why anchoring works.** Any line with `m` points passes through each of those `m` points. So when the anchor *happens* to be one of them, every other point on that line produces the *same* slope relative to the anchor and lands in the same bucket. We don't need to try every line explicitly — fixing each point as an anchor in turn guarantees that, for the maximal line, at least one of its points serves as anchor and sees all the others. That's why a single hashed pass per anchor, `O(n²)` total, suffices instead of the `O(n³)` triple scan.

**Why the slope must be an exact integer vector, not a float.** The naive key `slope = dy / dx` has two fatal flaws. First, **division by zero** on vertical lines where `dx = 0`. Second, and subtler, **floating-point imprecision**: most ratios (e.g. `1/3`) aren't representable exactly in binary floating point, so two points that are genuinely collinear can produce slightly different `double` slopes and split into separate buckets — or two distinct lines can round to the same value and merge. Geometry demands exactness, so we keep the slope as the integer pair `(dx, dy)` and never divide into a real number.

**Why reduce by the gcd.** Points farther from the anchor along the same line have proportionally larger `(dx, dy)` — e.g. `(1,2)`, `(2,4)`, `(3,6)` all describe the same direction. Dividing both components by `g = gcd(dx, dy)` collapses them to the single reduced vector `(1,2)`, so every point on that line hashes to one bucket regardless of how far out it sits. Without the gcd reduction, collinear-but-different-distance points would scatter across buckets and the count would be wrong.

**Why normalize the sign.** Even after gcd reduction, a direction and its opposite are the same line: `(1,2)` and `(−1,−2)` point along the same line through the anchor. To make them collide we choose one canonical orientation — force `dx > 0`; when `dx == 0` (a vertical line) force `dy > 0`. Concretely, negate both components when `dx < 0`, or when `dx == 0 && dy < 0`. This guarantees `(2,1)` and `(−2,−1)` share a key and a line isn't accidentally counted as two.

**Why `bucket + 1` and the `n <= 2` guard.** Each bucket counts only the *other* points sharing that slope; the anchor itself lies on the line too, so the line's size is `bucket + 1`. And with `n <= 2` the inner loop may never form a bucket, so we return `n` directly — one or two points are trivially collinear.

**Why uniqueness simplifies things.** Older variants allowed duplicate points, forcing a separate 'identical coordinate' counter added to *every* line through the anchor. Here points are guaranteed unique, so `(dx, dy)` is never `(0, 0)` for `j != i` and the gcd is always positive — no special duplicate bookkeeping needed.
approaches.insight: The whole optimisation is 'group by an exact direction'. A hash map turns the geometric question 'are these collinear with the anchor?' into 'do they hash to the same reduced vector?'. The reusable craft is the *key design*: gcd-reduce to make scale irrelevant, sign-normalize to make orientation irrelevant. Any time you group by a ratio or direction — parallel lines, equivalent fractions, reflection symmetry — this exact-key recipe beats floating point.

diagrams.title: Building an exact slope key
diagrams.caption: From raw difference vector to a canonical hashable key: reduce by gcd, then normalize the sign.

edgeCases.behavior: Vertical line: dx = 0 each time; sign-normalize forces dy > 0 so all share key (0,1) → returns 3.
Horizontal line: dy = 0; gcd reduces dx to 1, key (1,0) for all → returns 3.
Anchor (2,3): (3,3) gives (1,0); (−5,3) gives dx=−7→ normalize → (1,0). Same bucket → collinear, returns 3.

pitfalls: Keying on `(double) dy / dx` — float imprecision splits/merges lines and crashes on vertical dx = 0.
Skipping gcd reduction — collinear points at different distances scatter into different buckets.
Skipping sign normalization — a line splits into two buckets for its two directions.
Forgetting `+1` for the anchor, or starting `best` such that the trivial 2-point line is missed.
Reusing one slope map across anchors instead of resetting per anchor.

commonMistakes: Using floating-point slope dy/dx as the hash key — precision errors and vertical-line divide-by-zero.
Not reducing the difference vector by gcd, so collinear points at different distances land in different buckets.
Not normalizing the sign, so a single line is counted as two opposite-direction buckets.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Floating-point slope key
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Most ratios aren't exactly representable as doubles, so genuinely collinear points can produce different slopes (splitting a line) or distinct lines can round equal (merging them). Vertical lines also divide by zero. Use an exact integer vector key.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to normalize the sign
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After gcd reduction, (1,2) and (-1,-2) describe the same line through the anchor but hash differently, so the line is split into two undercounted buckets. Pick a canonical orientation.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
g = math.gcd(dx, dy)
dx //= g
dy //= g
key = (dx, dy)   # (1,2) and (-1,-2) become different keys
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
g = math.gcd(dx, dy)
dx //= g
dy //= g
if dx < 0 or (dx == 0 and dy < 0):
    dx, dy = -dx, -dy
key = (dx, dy)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the +1 for the anchor
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The slope bucket only counts the *other* points sharing that direction. The anchor lies on the line too, so the line's true size is bucket + 1. Omitting it undercounts every line by one.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
slopes[key] = slopes.get(key, 0) + 1
best = max(best, slopes[key])        # misses the anchor
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
slopes[key] = slopes.get(key, 0) + 1
best = max(best, slopes[key] + 1)    # +1 for the anchor itself

patternNote: The canonical 'anchor + hash an exact ratio' geometry pattern. Recognise it whenever you must group points by a slope, direction, or fraction and floating point would corrupt the comparison. The defining moves are the per-anchor sweep and the gcd-reduced, sign-normalized integer key; the same exact-key discipline powers Line Reflection, Number of Boomerangs, and Check If It Is a Straight Line.
